title: PnW Play Type
description: Find the Politics & War playstyle you naturally lean toward: raiding, farming, diplomacy, strategy, stats, banking, building, or frontline war.

raider.label: Raider
raider.summary: You thrive on opportunistic offensive wars, inactive targets, loot math, beige timing, and turning MAPs into profit.

farmer.label: Farmer
farmer.summary: You prefer stable production, resource planning, low-drama growth, and making your nation economically reliable.

diplomat.label: Diplomat
diplomat.summary: You play the relationship game: reputation, treaty webs, de-escalation, coalition awareness, and careful communication.

strategist.label: Strategist
strategist.summary: You think in doctrine, timing, ranges, blitz plans, alliance objectives, and how individual moves affect the wider board.

stats_master.label: Stats Master
stats_master.summary: You love score ranges, war data, activity patterns, net damage, beige cycles, and turning raw numbers into decisions.

banker.label: Banker
banker.summary: You naturally manage liquidity, grants, taxes, repayment risk, resource exposure, and alliance financial discipline.

builder.label: Builder
builder.summary: You are growth-focused: city timing, infra levels, projects, improvements, commerce, and efficient long-term scaling.

warfighter.label: Warfighter
warfighter.summary: You like coordinated combat: units, resistance, control, counters, air superiority, naval pressure, and executing orders cleanly.

questions.prompt: You log in and have two open offensive war slots. What do you check first?

answers.text: Inactive targets with cash/resources exposed and weak military.
Alliance target lists and whether a counter chain needs another hit.
Whether declaring would hurt an active diplomatic situation.
Whether staying peaceful protects my revenue and build plan.

questions.prompt: Your alliance posts a city grant program. Your strongest instinct is to:

answers.text: Check bank liquidity, repayment risk, eligibility, and audit trail.
Calculate whether the new city beats infra/project spending right now.
Ask how the program affects war range and tier consolidation.
Take it if it helps production and keep my nation boringly profitable.

questions.prompt: True or false: In raid wars, loot potential and target inactivity usually matter more than winning a pretty war screen.

answers.text: True
False

questions.prompt: A treaty partner complains about one of your alliance's raids. You would rather:

answers.text: Get facts, calm the room, and keep the relationship intact.
Review whether the target was legal and if a counter is likely.
Measure the actual damage, loot, and activity before reacting.
Ask whether the raid was worth risking future trade/security.

questions.prompt: Which dashboard would you keep open during a global war?

answers.text: Target slots, MAPs, resistance, beige timers, and counter status.
Net damage, unit losses, active nations, and tier-by-tier outcomes.
Coalition channels, diplomatic commitments, and escalation risk.
Bank outflows, rebuild exposure, and resource burn rates.

questions.prompt: Your nation has extra cash. What feels like the best use?

answers.text: Buy the next city or a project that improves long-term scaling.
Keep reserves so I can rebuy units, rebuild, or cover tax needs.
Fund military and go find profitable raid targets.
Increase infra/improvements to make income steadier.

questions.prompt: True or false: A good war plan should account for score range, blitz timing, target priority, counters, and beige control.

answers.text: True
False

questions.prompt: Which PnW mechanic do you enjoy optimizing most?

answers.text: MAP usage and resistance damage during active wars.
City count, infra, land, commerce, and project order.
Trade prices, tax flow, grants, and resource reserves.
Loot odds, target activity, and offensive slot uptime.

questions.prompt: A nation in your tier is low on aircraft but has tanks and ships. What do you think?

answers.text: Can I exploit air superiority or force bad rebuy choices?
How does hitting them affect the tier's broader war plan?
What do their stats say about activity and likely response time?
Would opening this war create a diplomatic headache?

questions.prompt: Which peacetime goal sounds most like you?

answers.text: Grow cities/projects efficiently and avoid wasting cash on bad timing.
Produce reliably, keep bills paid, and avoid unnecessary risk.
Improve alliance relationships and reduce future conflict risk.
Build better reports for activity, growth, war readiness, and trade.

questions.prompt: True or false: Keeping accurate bank records is gameplay power because it affects grants, rebuilds, taxes, and trust.

answers.text: True
False

questions.prompt: A weaker nation declares on you. Your preferred response is:

answers.text: Punish the mistake with efficient attacks and deny their win condition.
Check if they are bait or part of a larger operation before reacting.
Estimate whether looting them back makes the war profitable.
Ask if peace is cleaner than wasting resources.

questions.prompt: What makes a target attractive?

answers.text: Large exposed loot, bad military, inactive recent activity.
High strategic value to the war plan, not just personal profit.
A clean data profile showing they are the right hit.
A target that will not create avoidable FA trouble.

questions.prompt: When resource prices swing, you are most likely to:

answers.text: Rebalance stockpiles and protect alliance liquidity.
Adjust production/improvements for steadier profit.
Look for whether war demand signals a coming conflict.
Check whether raiding can source resources cheaper than buying.

questions.prompt: True or false: Diplomacy in PnW can be as decisive as military strength because treaties and reputation shape who gets isolated.

answers.text: True
False

questions.prompt: What do you do after a war ends?

answers.text: Review damage, performance, activity, and missed opportunities.
Rebuild units and prepare for the next round.
Plan city/project growth around the rebuild window.
Help repair relationships and shape the post-war narrative.

questions.prompt: Pick the report you would most want to maintain.

answers.text: Inactive profitable raid targets by range and loot.
City/project ROI and build recommendations.
Treaty map, bloc movement, and embassy contact quality.
Bank balances, grants, taxes, resource stockpiles, and repayments.

questions.prompt: How do you feel about infra?

answers.text: It should be bought with ROI, risk, and war exposure in mind.
It is income stability as long as I am not about to get burned.
It is loot someone else may donate if they overbuild and go inactive.
It changes score range, so it affects target matching and tier shape.

questions.prompt: True or false: Score range and tier shape can matter more than a single nation's raw strength.

answers.text: True
False

questions.prompt: Your alliance asks for a military rebuy. What question do you ask?

answers.text: What units are needed for our actual targets and control goals?
How much will this cost the bank and who needs aid?
What does this do to my economy if the war drags?
Can I use the rebuy to hit better loot targets too?

questions.prompt: Which phrase most sounds like your PnW brain?

answers.text: What is the expected value of this hit?
What does this do to the treaty web?
What is the cleanest growth path from here?
What do the numbers say after sample size?

questions.prompt: A small alliance asks yours for protection. You focus on:

answers.text: Their reliability, reputation, and whether the relationship is worth it.
Whether their tier helps or hurts future military options.
Whether defending them creates expensive obligations.
Whether they are active enough to avoid becoming raid bait.

questions.prompt: True or false: A farmer playstyle still needs enough military awareness to avoid being easy profit for raiders.

answers.text: True
False

questions.prompt: What kind of alliance project would you volunteer for?

answers.text: A raiding finder with inactivity, loot, military, and range filters.
A build optimizer for city, infra, project, and improvement order.
A foreign affairs map of relationships and conflict risk.
A bank ledger with grant eligibility and resource exposure alerts.

questions.prompt: During a blitz, your favorite job is:

answers.text: Hit assigned targets fast and follow MAP timing.
Track who declared, who missed, and where counters are needed.
Adjust the plan when target availability changes.
Make sure allies and partners understand the operation boundaries.

questions.prompt: Which mistake annoys you most?

answers.text: Leaving profitable inactive targets untouched for days.
Buying cities/projects in a wasteful order.
Making public comments that damage diplomatic options.
Making claims without checking the data.

questions.prompt: True or false: Coordinated counters are usually stronger than scattered revenge hits.

answers.text: True
False

questions.prompt: Your preferred risk profile is:

answers.text: High activity, high upside, frequent wars if the loot is real.
Low chaos, steady growth, strong reserves.
Calculated alliance-level risk for long-term position.
Measured risk backed by logs, charts, and observed behavior.

questions.prompt: When choosing improvements, you care most about:

answers.text: Production and commerce that fit my peaceful income plan.
Military capacity and whether my MMR fits alliance policy.
Long-term build efficiency across cities and projects.
How the build compares statistically to similar nations.

questions.prompt: What makes a PnW session feel successful?

answers.text: I found targets, used slots, and came away richer.
My nation grew cleanly and my income plan improved.
A tense situation got calmer because communication was handled well.
The alliance made better decisions because the numbers were clear.

questions.prompt: If your alliance loses a war, your first constructive thought is:

answers.text: Which tactical choices cost resistance, units, or control?
Which strategic assumption was wrong before the first declare?
How do we finance rebuilds without wrecking growth?
How do we recover morale and stabilize production?

questions.prompt: Choose the title that feels most like home.

answers.text: The player who can turn war slots into money.
The player whose nation grows predictably and efficiently.
The player who understands the map before everyone else does.
The player who converts data and mechanics into wins.
